title: Security Reference Architecture for Cloud Data Mirrors
text:
Cloud Data Mirror RFC: your data, encrypted with your key, readable only by the AI you approve









Request for comments. Round 1 is open until 11 December 2026, 23:59 UTC.



What this is. A security reference architecture for cloud data mirrors: a private copy of a person’s messages and data that only the readers they choose, including their AI assistants, can search. AJS Consult LLC publishes it for open review.
How to take part

Read it. Start with the executive summary.
Comment or suggest changes. On any page: select text to comment on it, press Suggest edits to change the wording right on the page and send your changes, or comment at the end of the page. Suggestions and comments made with a GitHub account are credited to it.
Follow the review. Updates: sign up by email, use the feed, or watch on GitHub.
Found a security problem in the running service? Email aaron@matterboard.ai with SECURITY in the subject. Never post it in a comment.




Round 1





Opens

A request for comments (RFC) on encrypting private data mirrors so that a copy of the stored data is useless on its own, and the data opens only while a device or AI the user approved is making a request.

title: 2. Executive summary
text:
Comment or suggest a change. Select any text to comment on it. Press Suggest edits to change the wording right on this page, then send your changes. Or comment at the end of the page with your GitHub account.
Suggest edits
How suggestions are credited · Edit the Markdown on GitHub

Today, AI assistants connect directly to a user’s private correspondence via a variety of partially and fully supported, secure (and insecure) connectors. Under this status quo, AI providers become the custodians of this data, to the end of enabling bleeding edge automation and research capabilities to their users. Simply put, users should not need to hand over custody of their data in exchange for access to the best AIs. This document proposes a security architecture for a messaging mirror that can be securely, safely and privately operated by the user themselves or by a trusted 3rd party.
The proposal. One random key is made on the user’s own computer, and messages are encrypted there before they are uploaded. Each device or AI the user approves gets its own token, and the server can open the data only while one of them is making a request, so a copy of the database alone is useless. This is not end-to-end encryption: the server sees what it serves while it serves it, and What it does not protect lists the limits.
The problem. Data ownership concerns are among the most significant impediments to the proliferation of beneficial AI, especially in security, safety and privacy critical use cases. There currently exists no complete security reference architecture to enable individuals or organizations to securely, safely and privately host their own data mirrors in a way that is integrated and compatible with AI assistants. Closed-source solutions to data mirroring require users to trust the implementation, and this document is meant to align users on “the right way” to achieve this goal so trust can be attained.
The alternative. Without a community effort to develop a security, privacy and safety standard around private data, the most likely outcome is for AIs to become more entrenched in their position as system of record for user’s private data optimally stored for use by AI. Private 3rd party companies hosting closed source messaging mirrors require the user to trust that bond, which is a non-starter for anyone hosting sensitive or mission critical data. As well, the technical requirements of building such data management systems require seasoned, credentialed software engineering veterans and are thus costly and/or out of reach for most potential users of powerful AI.
What is asked of you. Help us figure out what’s worth building that will actually get adopted because it is trusted. Attack the design. What it does not protect, the search leakage (question 1) and the questions for reviewers matter most.

title: 3. What it defends against
text:
Comment or suggest a change. Select any text to comment on it. Press Suggest edits to change the wording right on this page, then send your changes. Or comment at the end of the page with your GitHub account.
Suggest edits
How suggestions are credited · Edit the Markdown on GitHub

The design has one goal: a copy of the stored data is useless without a credential the user approved. It does not hide data from the server while the server answers an approved request.







Who
Protected?




Someone who steals the database, a backup or a disk
Yes. They hold ciphertext, search tags and token hashes, and no key. The tags still leak some structure (see What it does not protect). Attachments are encrypted by the storage service under a key it does not keep, so a copy of the bucket is unreadable as well.


The operator’s staff reading stored data
Yes, in the same way


A reader or writer after the user revokes it
Yes, through the service: its token no longer finds a copy


A compromised server, or an operator who changes the server’s code
No. It sees the account key during any approved request and could keep it.


Malware on the user’s desktop
No. The desktop holds the account key.

title: 4. System Requirements
text:
Comment or suggest a change. Select any text to comment on it. Press Suggest edits to change the wording right on this page, then send your changes. Or comment at the end of the page with your GitHub account.
Suggest edits
How suggestions are credited · Edit the Markdown on GitHub

The design exists to meet five requirements, and nothing in it serves anything else.








#
Requirement
How the design meets it




R1
The user controls the keys
The account key is made on the user’s desktop. A reader or writer gets access only when the user approves it, and loses it when the user revokes it.


R2
The desktop sync app collects and pushes messages in real time, encrypted from the source
The app encrypts each message under a content key derived from the account key, and computes its search tags, before it uploads. The server never receives plaintext from the app. Attachments are the exception (see Decisions made to simplify).


R3
Data is secure at rest in the database
The database holds ciphertext, keyed tags and token hashes. Nothing in it opens without a token.


R4
Approved readers and writers can search, retrieve and update in near real time
Each holds a token that opens its own copy of the account key for one request. A message is searchable as soon as it is stored.


R5
Under 10 seconds from a user’s question to the AI’s first response
The mirror’s share is budgeted at 1 second at the 95th percentile. The rest belongs to the AI.

title: 5. The design on one page
text:
Comment or suggest a change. Select any text to comment on it. Press Suggest edits to change the wording right on this page, then send your changes. Or comment at the end of the page with your GitHub account.
Suggest edits
How suggestions are credited · Edit the Markdown on GitHub

There is one key, one kind of token, and two algorithms: AES-256-GCM encrypts everything, and SHA-256 does the rest as a hash, as HMAC and as HKDF. Everything else follows from them.


Figure 5.1. The whole design: one account key, one kind of token, a database and a blob store · Text version 

One key. On installation, the desktop sync application asks the operating system for 256 random bits, and those bits are the “account key”. The user’s OS key store holds the account key and releases it only to approved application(s). The account key never encrypts anything itself. Instead, HKDF-SHA256 turns it into two working keys, one per job: (1) a content key that encrypts each message (AES-256-GCM) and (2) a tag key that computes the search tags (HMAC-SHA256). A third, the storage key, is derived the same way for attachments. They are re-derived whenever they are needed, so nothing extra is stored, and learning one working key reveals neither the other nor the account key. Because both come from the one account key, a reader that can open its copy of the account key can both read messages and search them.


Why this is current best practice: a full-strength random key from an approved generator (NIST SP 800-133 Rev. 2); one key per purpose, never one key for two jobs (NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5, key separation); and working keys derived with HKDF (RFC 5869), the extract-then-expand construction NIST approves in SP 800-56C Rev. 2 and the one TLS 1.3 uses for all its keys (RFC 8446).


Encrypted at the source. The desktop app encrypts each message with AES-256-GCM, bound to the account and the message’s id, and computes its search tags with HMAC-SHA256. Only ciphertext and tags leave the desktop. Attachments are the exception: the desktop uploads them as they are, and the storage service encrypts each one under a storage key that is derived from the account key, supplied with the request and never kept (see Decisions made to simplify).


Why this is current best practice: AES-256-GCM is the NIST-approved authenticated encryption mode (SP 800-38D, over AES in FIPS 197), so tampering is detected, not just hidden. Binding each ciphertext to its account and message id as associated data follows the AEAD design in RFC 5116, which stops a stored ciphertext being swapped into another row or account. HMAC-SHA256 is the approved keyed hash (FIPS 198-1), and keyed tags over fragments are the classic construction for search over encrypted data (Song, Wagner and Perrig, IEEE S&P 2000). Its known limit, that equal fragments produce equal tags, is question 1, and GCM’s nonce limit is question 2.


One kind of token. Every reader or writer the user approves gets a random 256-bit token: a connected AI, the web app, a second device, a script. The server keeps the token’s SHA-256, to find it, and one copy of the account key locked under a key derived from the token (AES-256-GCM, the cipher that also encrypts messages). One token, one copy.


Why this is current best practice: high-entropy bearer tokens are the OAuth standard (RFC 6750), and short lifetimes with refresh-token rotation follow the OAuth security best current practice (RFC 9700). Keeping only a hash of each token means a database copy yields no usable credential, the same rule NIST SP 800-63B sets for stored passwords. Locking one copy of the account key per holder with AES-256-GCM, an authenticated cipher that NIST also approves for wrapping keys (NIST SP 800-38F) is envelope encryption, the pattern cloud key-management services use.


Search without plaintext. Inside an approved request the server unlocks the account key, turns the query into tags, finds candidates in an ordinary database index, and decrypts only those.


Why this is current best practice: keyed tags are the standard construction for search over encrypted data (Song, Wagner and Perrig, IEEE S&P 2000). Filtering on trigrams and then checking the real match is how production regex search works (Russ Cox, Regular Expression Matching with a Trigram Index). The known cost is access-pattern leakage (Cash et al., Leakage-Abuse Attacks Against Searchable Encryption, CCS 2015), which is why this design names it as a limit and asks reviewers about it (question 1).


Revocation is deletion. Deleting a token’s hash and its copy cuts that reader or writer off at once.


Why this is current best practice: revoking one holder deletes its only way to open the key through the service. Deleting every copy, as account deletion does, is cryptographic erase, a sanitization method NIST recognizes (SP 800-88 Rev. 1). Revoking a token server-side, effective on its next use, is what OAuth token revocation specifies (RFC 7009). Two gaps remain: backups hold old copies for up to 30 days, and the other copies of the same key stay valid (see What it does not protect).

The server never stores the account key, a token or plaintext. It holds the account key in memory only while it answers a request from an approved token.
One rule for every credential. Each credential has its own locked copy of the account key. Every hand-off opens the copy with the old credential, locks a new copy under the new one, and deletes the old. An OAuth authorization code, the web app’s connect code and a renewed token are all hand-offs of this kind, so the server never needs to store a token while one is in transit. A recovery code is the same thing on paper.

title: 6. How it works
text:
6.1 Key management lifecycle
The same machinery seen twice: first what happens to the account key, then what happens to the data.
The account key is created once on the desktop, opened only inside approved requests, changed only by adding or removing locked copies, and destroyed by deleting every copy.
Figure 6.1. Where the account key lives in the clear, and where only locked copies exist · Text version
Only a desktop keystore holds the account key at rest. The server holds it in memory for one request at a time; everything else holds a locked copy, a token, or nothing.
Every change to who can read the mirror is a copy of the account key added or deleted; the account key itself changes only if it is rotated.

title: 6. How it works
text:
6.1.1 Create
On first run, the desktop app generates the account key from 256 random bits and stores it in the OS keystore. It then signs in, receives its own desktop token, wraps the account key under a key derived from that token, and uploads only that locked copy. The server stores the copy beside the token’s hash; it never sees the account key and never keeps the token.


Figure 6.2. Create: the desktop makes the account key and uploads only a locked copy · Text version 
Why this is best practice. The key is made from a cryptographically secure random source on the device that will hold it, which is what NIST SP 800-133 Rev. 2 recommends, and it is stored in the OS key store, hardware-backed where the platform offers it, rather than in a file. The server receives only a wrapped copy (NIST SP 800-38F), so nothing the server stores can open the data. That separation is the core idea of client-side and envelope encryption.


6.1.2 Read
A reader’s request carries its token. The server finds the reader’s locked copy by the token’s hash, derives the unwrapping key from the token with HKDF, and opens the account key in memory. It looks up the query’s tags, decrypts only the candidate rows and returns the results. When the request ends, the account key is dropped; nothing of it is written to disk or logs.


Figure 6.3. Read: a token opens its copy of the account key for one request · Text version 
Why this is best practice. The key is opened only in memory, only for one request, and then dropped. That follows NIST SP 800-57 Part 1: keep plaintext keys out of persistent storage and out of logs, and limit how long they exist. The unwrapping key is derived from the token with HKDF (RFC 5869), the standard way to turn a high-entropy secret into a key, and the server looks tokens up by hash, so its stored data holds no usable credential.


6.1.3 Update
When the user approves a new reader or writer, the approval happens inside a session that already holds the account key. The server makes a new token, wraps the account key under a key derived from it, stores that copy beside the new token’s hash, and hands the new token to the new holder once. Renewing a token follows the same steps, then deletes the old token’s hash and copy. The account key itself does not change.


Figure 6.4. Update: a new reader or writer gets its own token and its own locked copy · Text version 
Why this is best practice. Granting access means wrapping the same key once more, not re-encrypting data or sharing one credential among holders. This is envelope encryption, the pattern cloud key-management services use, and it means every holder can be revoked on its own. Handing a new token over once and rotating it on renewal follows the OAuth security best current practice (RFC 9700).


6.1.4 Expire
Every token has an end time, stored beside its hash. The server refuses an expired token on every request, and a periodic sweep then deletes the expired token’s hash and its copy of the account key. A holder renews before its end time by presenting its current token, which follows Update; a refresh token presented twice revokes its whole chain. The lifetime for each kind of holder is question 4. Backups can still hold an expired copy for up to 30 days (see What it does not protect).


Figure 6.5. Expire: an expired token is refused and its copy is deleted · Text version 
Why this is best practice. Every token has a fixed lifetime, and its copy of the key is deleted when that lifetime ends, so a leaked token stops working without anyone acting. Bounded lifetimes are what RFC 9700 recommends for tokens, and NIST calls them cryptoperiods (SP 800-57 Part 1).


6.1.5 Delete
The user ends access in one of three ways, each from an approved device:

Revoke one reader or writer (an AI, a browser session, a script). The server deletes that token’s hash and its copy of the account key. That holder is cut off at once, and every other holder keeps working.
Remove a lost device. The same deletion, for the device’s token. Recovery then runs as an Update from a device the user still has.
Delete the account. The server deletes every copy and every row. With no copy of the account key left, nothing live can open the mirror.

Backups still hold old copies until they expire, up to 30 days. If every holder is lost, the next desktop makes a new account key and collects again from the sources.


Figure 6.6. Delete: access ends when a token’s hash and its copy are deleted · Text version 
Why this is best practice. Deleting every copy of the key, as account deletion does, is cryptographic erase, a sanitization method NIST recognizes (SP 800-88 Rev. 1). It works at once, even when ciphertext remains in storage the user cannot reach. Revoking a single holder is weaker: it ends that holder’s access through the service, but other copies of the same key remain. Revocation takes effect server-side on the token’s next use, as OAuth token revocation specifies (RFC 7009). The known exception is backups, which keep old copies for up to 30 days.

title: 6. How it works
text:
6.2 How data moves
Five flows cover everything the system does. In each one, the account key is opened only inside a request that presents an approved token.

6.2.1 Collect and push
New messages are locked on the user’s own computer before they go anywhere, so the service stores only ciphertext, which opens only inside an approved request.

The desktop app reads a new message from a source on the desktop: mail, messaging apps, team chat, a calendar.
It encrypts the message under the content key and computes its search tags under the tag key, both derived from the account key.
It uploads the ciphertext and tags over TLS, presenting its own token. The server stores them and cannot open them without an approved token.
The message is searchable as soon as it is stored.



Figure 6.7. Collect and push: messages are encrypted on the desktop before upload · Text version 
Only ciphertext and tags leave the desktop; the server cannot open them without an approved token.
Why this is best practice. Encrypting on the client before upload, so the storage provider holds only ciphertext, is the model behind end-to-end encrypted storage and client-side encryption. Each message is sealed with AES-256-GCM (NIST SP 800-38D), an authenticated cipher that detects any change to the ciphertext, and it is bound to its account and message ids as associated data (RFC 5116), so a row cannot be moved to another account or message. TLS protects the upload in transit (RFC 8446).


6.2.2 Approve a reader or writer
Nothing gets access unless the user says yes, and every approved AI, browser or device gets its own key that can be cancelled on its own.

The user approves it: OAuth consent for an AI, the web app opened from the desktop, or a matching code for a second device.
Inside the user’s own approved session, the server makes a new token and a copy of the account key locked under it.
The token is handed to the new reader or writer once. The server keeps only its hash.



Figure 6.8. Approve a reader or writer: one approval, one token, one locked copy · Text version 
The server keeps only the token’s hash; the token itself is handed over once.
Why this is best practice. AI clients are approved through OAuth consent with PKCE, as the OAuth security best current practice requires (RFC 9700), and a second device is approved by comparing a short code on both screens, a relative of the device flow in RFC 8628. Giving each holder its own token and its own wrapped copy of the key is least privilege: no credential is shared, so each one can be revoked alone. Storing only a hash of each token means a database copy yields no usable credential, as NIST SP 800-63B requires for stored passwords.


6.2.3 Search and retrieve
An approved AI gets answers in well under a second, and the data is unlocked only for that one question, then locked again.

A reader sends a query with its token.
The server finds the token’s copy by its hash and unlocks the account key for this request.
It turns the query into tags, finds the candidates in the index, decrypts only those, and checks the real match.
It returns the results and drops the account key.



Figure 6.9. Search and retrieve: the account key is opened for one request only · Text version 
Only the candidate rows are decrypted, and the account key lives only for the request.
Why this is best practice. Search runs on keyed tags, the standard construction for searching encrypted data (Song, Wagner and Perrig, IEEE S&P 2000). The query is reduced to trigrams and the real match is checked afterwards, as in production regex search (Russ Cox, trigram index). Holding the key in memory for one request only follows NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 on limiting how long plaintext keys exist. The known cost is access-pattern leakage (Cash et al., CCS 2015), which question 1 puts to reviewers.


6.2.4 Update
Edits by an approved AI or by the user are locked the moment they are saved, and every other reader sees them on its next request.

A writer sends a change with its token: an AI’s tool call, or an edit on the web app.
The server unlocks the account key, encrypts the change, recomputes its tags and stores it.
Every reader sees it on its next request.



Figure 6.10. Update: a writer’s change is encrypted on the server inside its request · Text version 
Writes follow the same rule as reads: the account key is opened only inside the writer’s request.
Why this is best practice. A write uses the same authenticated encryption as a read, so the server never stores an edited row in the clear. Every write gets a fresh random nonce, which is what keeps AES-GCM secure when the same key encrypts many messages (NIST SP 800-38D, section 8). The tags are recomputed with HMAC-SHA256 (FIPS 198-1), so the search index never falls out of step with the content.


6.2.5 Revoke and recover
Cutting off an AI or a lost device takes effect at once and touches no one else; a replacement device is approved like any other.

Revoke. Deleting a token’s hash and copy cuts that reader or writer off at once.
A lost desktop. From another approved device the user revokes it, then approves a new desktop, which receives the account key through its own copy.
The only desktop lost. A recovery code made at setup is one more token, printed and kept offline, with its own locked copy. Presented from a new desktop, it approves that desktop. Without one, the mirror starts again with a new account key even if AI readers still hold tokens, because a reader’s token cannot approve a device.
Every holder lost. The mirror cannot be read. A new desktop makes a new account key and collects again from the sources.



Figure 6.11. Revoke and recover: one deletion cuts a holder off, and recovery needs another approved device · Text version 
Cutting off a reader is one deletion; a replacement desktop is approved like any other holder.
Why this is best practice. Revoking a token server-side, so that it fails on its next use, is what OAuth token revocation specifies (RFC 7009). Deleting that token’s copy ends its access through the service. Only deleting every copy is cryptographic erase, the sanitization method NIST recognizes (SP 800-88 Rev. 1). Recovering through another approved device, rather than through a reset the operator controls, keeps the operator unable to open the data. End-to-end encrypted services use the same approach, and when every holder is lost the honest result is that the data cannot be read.

title: 7. Latency budget
text:
Comment or suggest a change. Select any text to comment on it. Press Suggest edits to change the wording right on this page, then send your changes. Or comment at the end of the page with your GitHub account.
Suggest edits
How suggestions are credited · Edit the Markdown on GitHub

Encryption costs the answer well under a second: the mirror’s whole share is targeted at 0.4 seconds, inside a 1-second budget, so most of the 10 seconds belongs to the AI.


Figure 7.1. Latency budget: targets at the 95th percentile, not measurements · Text version 
These are targets, not measurements. Before launch they are measured on a synthetic account the size of the largest real one, about 1.6 million messages. A new message is searchable once its upload completes; the target is under 2 seconds from arriving on the desktop.

title: 8. What it does not protect
text:
Comment or suggest a change. Select any text to comment on it. Press Suggest edits to change the wording right on this page, then send your changes. Or comment at the end of the page with your GitHub account.
Suggest edits
How suggestions are credited · Edit the Markdown on GitHub

This is encryption controlled by the user’s keys, not end-to-end encryption: the server decrypts inside each approved request. The limits follow.







Limit
Consequence




The server holds the account key and the results while it answers
A compromised server can capture the account key from any approved request. That one key opens the whole mirror, past and future, until the key is rotated. Proving which code the server runs (attestation) would close this; it is not in this design.


AI providers see what they retrieve
Their handling of results is outside this design


Search tags reveal which messages share a fragment
The tags are deterministic and overlap, so a thief of the database may recover text from fragment frequencies alone, and more with some known plaintext (question 1). Sizes and times are visible too.


A stolen token works until it is revoked
Expiry limits the damage (question 4)


Malware on the desktop sees everything
The desktop holds the account key


Backups keep deleted copies until they expire
A revoked token can still open its copy in a backup taken earlier, for up to 30 days


Revoking one holder is access control, not erasure
Other copies of the same key remain, and a holder that paired its token with a copy of the database keeps the key. Only deleting every copy, or rotating the key, erases.


Every token opens the whole account key
What a holder may do (read only, one source, approve others) is enforced by the server’s rules, not by cryptography


Tokens, queries and results are plaintext in the server’s memory
They must be kept out of logs, traces and error reports. Whatever ends TLS in front of the server sees tokens too. Mitigation: the implementation’s source code is published, and automated tests plant marker values in tokens, queries and results and fail if a marker reaches a log, a trace, an error report or stored data. Publishing the source shows what the code does; proving that the running server is that code is what attestation would add (question 7).


The mirror is only as fresh as the desktop
While the desktop is off or asleep, nothing new is collected


Search needs a fixed fragment of three or more characters
A query without one cannot use the index. It must be refused, or answered by decrypting every row.


Attachments are encrypted by the storage service, not on the desktop
The storage service sees each file in the clear while it handles an upload or a read. At rest, a file opens only with the storage key, which is derived from the account key inside an approved request. The bucket’s access policy stays as a second line.

title: 9. Decisions made to simplify
text:
Comment or suggest a change. Select any text to comment on it. Press Suggest edits to change the wording right on this page, then send your changes. Or comment at the end of the page with your GitHub account.
Suggest edits
How suggestions are credited · Edit the Markdown on GitHub

These choices keep the design small. Each has a cost, stated here so reviewers can challenge it.








Decision
What it removes
What it costs




Every source is collected on the desktop
Server-side collectors, and the public-key sealing they needed for mail that arrives while nobody is calling
A source that can only be read server-side, such as a hosted inbox or a chat bot, is out of scope until it can run on the desktop


The token is its own secret
Separate unlock secrets. SHA-256 of the token finds its copy; a key derived from the token with HKDF opens it, and knowing one gives nothing about the other.
A leaked token both identifies and unlocks, exactly as a leaked token-and-secret pair did before


Support is just another reader
The operator’s hardware-held support key. To get help, the user approves a support reader with an end time, like any other.
Its use is recorded in the service’s own log rather than by the cloud provider’s audit log


Background AI work needs a reader
Server-side processing with no request open. Triage or filing runs on the desktop, or inside a reader’s request.
Nothing is processed while every reader is idle


Attachments are encrypted by the storage service, under a key derived from the account key
Encrypting and chunking every file on the desktop
The storage service sees each file in the clear while it handles a request, and it must accept a key supplied per request. The bucket cannot hand out direct links, because every read needs the key.

title: 10. Questions for reviewers
text:
Comment or suggest a change. Select any text to comment on it. Press Suggest edits to change the wording right on this page, then send your changes. Or comment at the end of the page with your GitHub account.
Suggest edits
How suggestions are credited · Edit the Markdown on GitHub

These seven are where review is wanted most.

Search leakage. Is a keyed trigram index acceptable for this threat model, or should tag sets be padded?
Nonce budget. One content key encrypts every message for the account’s life with random 96-bit nonces, and NIST SP 800-38D limits that to 2³² uses per key. The largest account today holds about 1.6 million messages, far below that. Proposed answer: derive a new content key each year with HKDF from the account key and the year, so the limit applies per year and nothing extra is stored. Is that enough, or is a cipher that tolerates nonce reuse (AES-GCM-SIV, XAES-256-GCM) still worth adding?
Rotating the account key. Proposed answer: rotation is a re-push. The desktop makes a new account key, re-encrypts the mirror under it, including what writers added, uploads it again and deletes the old copies. That is the same path as when every holder is lost. It costs a full upload, so it is for a suspected compromise, not a schedule. Is that acceptable, or are data keys wrapped by the account key worth their extra machinery?
Token lifetimes. What expiry and renewal should each kind have: desktop, AI access and refresh, web app session, script?
A second desktop. Is a matching code shown on both screens enough to approve one? And how should the new desktop’s token reach it without the server storing it: handed to a waiting request in memory, or sealed to a key the new desktop sends?
Support audit. Is the service’s own log enough for support access, or is an independent audit worth a second key?
Attestation. Is proving which code the server runs worth adding later, to close the first limit?

title: Appendix A — Single or multi-tenant
text:

For stored data the choice barely matters, because each user’s rows are locked under that user’s own key. It matters for the server’s memory, for cost, and for who can see metadata.









One shared database
One database per user




Stored data
Isolated by each user’s key: another user’s rows, served by mistake, do not decrypt
The same, plus physical separation


A compromised server
Sees what every active user’s requests decrypt while it is compromised
Sees one user’s


Metadata: counts, sizes, times
Visible to the operator. Per-user tag keys stop matching across users.
Visible to whoever runs it


Deleting a user
Delete their copies of the account key and their rows
Delete the database


Cost and operations
One database to run
One per user





Figure A.1. One shared database compared with one database per user · Text version 
The recommendation is one codebase that runs either way. Shared by default, with row-level security in the database as a second line behind the keys. A dedicated instance, run by the operator or by the user, for anyone who wants the smaller blast radius. The keys stay with the user in both.

title: Appendix B — The diagrams as text
text:
Figure 5.1. The whole design: one account key, one kind of token, a database and a blob store
Every diagram in this document, written out: a description in words, for screen readers and search, and its source in Mermaid, which GitHub draws and anyone can edit in a pull request. The pictures in the chapters are exported from the editor’s document; these text versions are kept in step with them, and the sync tool reports any picture that has changed since its text version was last checked.
Plaintext exists only on the desktop and inside an approved request
In 5. The design on one page. One account key. The desktop encrypts messages before upload, and each reader or writer opens its own copy. The desktop app reads the sources on the desktop (mail, chats, calendars), makes and keeps the key, encrypts each message and computes search tags. It sends ciphertext and tags, and attachments as they are, to the server. Readers and writers (AI assistants, the web app, second devices and scripts), each with its own token, send a token and request to the server. The server finds the token’s copy, opens the key per request, searches and decrypts hits, returns the results and drops the key afterwards. It stores and looks up ciphertext, search tags, token hashes and locked copies of the key in the database, and stores and reads attachments in the blob store, encrypted under the storage key, which is sent with each request and never kept. The server never stores the account key, a token or plaintext. The blob store sees each attachment in the clear while it handles a request, and keeps only ciphertext.

title: Appendix B — The diagrams as text
section: Figure 6.1. Where the account key lives in the clear, and where only locked copies exist
text:
Figure 6.1. Where the account key lives in the clear, and where only locked copies exist
The account key exists in the clear in only two places
In 6. How it works. Where the account key lives, where only a locked copy lives, and where it never goes. In the clear, the key exists only in the desktop OS keystore, at rest on each approved desktop and made on the first one, and in server memory, with its two derived keys, for one approved request only. Only a locked copy is in the database, one copy per approved token wrapped under a key from it, and in backups, where deleted copies stay until the backup expires, up to 30 days. The AIs, board and scripts hold a token but never the key, and the server unlocks it for them. AI providers see only the results they asked for. Logs and operator staff hold no key, no token and no plaintext. A token opens only its own copy, so deleting that copy cuts its holder off at once.

title: Appendix B — The diagrams as text
section: Figure 6.2. Create: the desktop makes the account key and uploads only a locked copy
text:
Figure 6.2. Create: the desktop makes the account key and uploads only a locked copy
The account key is born on the desktop, and only a locked copy reaches the server
In 6. How it works. Create. The desktop app generates the account key from 256 random bits and stores it in the OS keystore. It signs in and asks the server for a desktop token, and the server replies with one. The desktop app wraps the account key under a key derived from the token and sends the locked copy to the server, which stores the token’s hash and the copy in the database. The account key never leaves the desktop in the clear.

section: Figure 6.3. Read: a token opens its copy of the account key for one request
text:
Figure 6.3. Read: a token opens its copy of the account key for one request
The account key is unwrapped for one request and never written down
In 6. How it works. Read. A reader or writer sends a request carrying its token. The server looks up the token’s hash in the database and gets back its locked copy. A key derived from the token unwraps the account key, in memory only. The server looks up the query’s tags and gets back ciphertext rows, decrypts the candidates and builds the answer, and returns the results. The request ends and the account key is dropped.

text:
Figure 6.4. Update: a new reader or writer gets its own token and its own locked copy
A new holder gets its own copy, made inside the user’s session
In 6. How it works. Update. The user approves a new reader or writer, inside a session that holds the account key. The server makes a new token and wraps the account key under a key derived from it, stores the new token’s hash and the copy in the database, and hands the new token to the reader or writer once. Renewal runs the same steps, then deletes the old token’s hash and copy.

section: Figure 6.5. Expire: an expired token is refused and its copy is deleted
text:
Figure 6.5. Expire: an expired token is refused and its copy is deleted
An expired token finds no copy and is refused
In 6. How it works. Expire. The server finds copies past their expiry in the database and deletes each one’s hash and copy. When a reader or writer then sends a request with the expired token, the server refuses it, and the holder must renew or be approved again. The account key itself is rotated before its nonce budget runs out, by re-encrypting or by re-wrapping data keys (questions 2 to 4).

text:
Figure 6.6. Delete: access ends when a token’s hash and its copy are deleted
Deleting copies is how access ends
In 6. How it works. Delete. The user revokes a token, or deletes the account. The server deletes that token’s hash and copy, or every copy and row. Backups keep old copies until they expire, up to 30 days. If every holder is lost, the next desktop makes a new account key and collects again.

text:
Figure 6.7. Collect and push: messages are encrypted on the desktop before upload
Messages are encrypted on the desktop before they leave it
In 6. How it works. Collect and push. The desktop app reads a new message from a local source, such as mail, chat or calendar. It encrypts the message under the account key and computes its search tags. It sends the ciphertext and tags to the server over TLS, with its token. The server stores them and cannot read them. The message is searchable as soon as it is stored.

Figure 6.9. Search and retrieve: the account key is opened for one request only
The account key is unlocked for one request and dropped when it ends
In 6. How it works. Search and retrieve. A reader or writer sends a query with its token. The server finds the token’s copy by its hash, unlocks the account key for this request and turns the query into tags. It finds the candidates in the index and gets back candidate rows, still ciphertext. It decrypts only the candidates, checks the real match, and returns the results. The request ends and the account key is dropped.

text:
Figure 6.11. Revoke and recover: one deletion cuts a holder off, and recovery needs another approved device
Revoking deletes a copy, and recovery needs another approved device
In 6. How it works. Revoke and recover. The user revokes a token, or a lost desktop, and the server deletes its hash and its copy in the database. A new desktop asks the server to join, the user approves the new desktop, and the server gives the new desktop its own token, which opens its own copy of the account key. If every holder is lost, the mirror cannot be read, and a new desktop makes a new account key and collects again from the sources.

title: Appendix B — The diagrams as text
section: Figure 7.1. Latency budget: targets at the 95th percentile, not measurements
text:
Figure 7.1. Latency budget: targets at the 95th percentile, not measurements
Encryption adds well under a second, and the answer lands inside the 10-second budget
In 7. Latency budget. Question to first response is 7.4 seconds at the 95th percentile, of which the mirror is 0.405 seconds. These are targets, not measurements. The AI provider reads the question and calls the mirror in an assumed 3 seconds. The mirror then takes 0.405 seconds of its 1-second budget: 0.2 seconds for the request to the server and back over the network, 0.005 seconds on the server to find the token and unlock the key, 0.1 seconds in the database to look up the query’s tags, and 0.1 seconds on the server to decrypt and check 200 candidates. The AI provider then writes the first words from the results in an assumed 4 seconds, so the first response arrives at 7.4 seconds, inside the 10-second budget.

title: Appendix B — The diagrams as text
section: Figure A.1. One shared database compared with one database per user
text:
Figure A.1. One shared database compared with one database per user
Keys isolate stored data either way, and separate instances contain a breach
In Appendix A. Single or multi-tenant. Each user’s key stays on their desktop in both designs, and colours mark whose key locks which rows. With one shared database, users A, B and C, holding keys A, B and C, all use one shared server, which opens key A, B or C inside each user’s request, and one shared database with row-level security, where user A’s rows are locked under key A, user B’s under key B and user C’s under key C. A server breach sees every active user’s requests. There is one system to run, and metadata is visible to the operator. With one instance per user, user A uses server A, which holds key A only, and database A, which holds user A’s rows under key A, and the same for users B and C. A server breach sees one user’s requests. There is one system per user to run and pay for.
